title: Gastrointestinal Disorders
markdown:
CHAPTER 7

## Gastrointestinal Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Abdominal pain
- Cholecystitis
- Acute appendicitis
- GERD
- Barrett's esophagus
- Diverticulitis
- Irritable bowel syndrome
- Diarrhea
- Colorectal cancer
- Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease
- Hepatitis
- Abdominal imaging

## NOTES

<!-- image -->

## THE ABDOMEN IS A POOR HISTORIAN

You must build a good differential diagnosis.

## Abdominal Pain Patterns

<!-- image -->

## Abdominal Pain: History

History is critical to understanding abdominal pain.

Important to ask a lot of questions:

- Where is the pain?
- When does the pain occur?
- Is the pain associated with other symptoms (nausea, vomiting, bowel movement)?
- Does anything relieve the pain?

## Abdominal Pain Clues

The source of pain may be "intra" or "extra" abdominal.

| Location             | Abdominal Differential Diagnosis                                                           | Extra-abdominal                        |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Epigastric           | Pancreatitis, gastric ulcer/ gastritis, GERD, hepatobiliary                                | Cardiac, pulmonary, vascular           |
| Right upper quadrant | Cholecystitis, acute hepatitis, others (hepatobiliary)                                     | Cardiac, pulmonary                     |
| Left upper quadrant  | Pancreatitis, PUD, GERD, gastritis, splenic                                                | Cardiac, vascular                      |
| Right lower quadrant | Appendicitis, nephrolithiasis, diverticulitis, IBS, IBD, pyelonephritis                    | Vascular, gynecologic, musculoskeletal |
| Left lower quadrant  | Appendicitis, diverticulitis, nephrolithiasis, pyelonephritis, IBD, IBS, colorectal cancer | Vascular, gynecologic, musculoskeletal |

## LET'S MEET OUR FIRST PATIENT!

## QUESTION #1

A 42-year-old female patient with obesity presents to the office with nausea, vomiting, and severe epigastric pain. Her symptoms started shortly after eating a hamburger. What diagnosis is most likely?

1. Diverticulitis
2. Peptic ulcer
3. Appendicitis
4. Acute cholecystitis

## Acute Cholecystitis

- Inflammation of the gallbladder
- Presentation
- $ RUQ pain: steady and severe
- $ "Colicky" sometimes epigastric or radiating to right shoulder
- $ High-fat meal causes pain
- $ Fever
- $ Movement makes the pain worse
- Commonly caused by gallstones
- $ Acalculous cholecystitis 5-10% cases

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES

## QUESTION #2

A patient with acute cholecystitis experiences inspiratory arrest when the right upper quadrant is palpated. What is this called?

1. Rovsing's sign
2. Murphy's sign
3. McBurney's sign
4. Kehr's sign

<!-- image -->

## Murphy's Sign

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #3

Which of the following is the preferred imaging study for diagnosis of acute cholecystitis?

1. Abdominal CT with contrast
2. Cholescintigraphy
3. Abdominal US
4. KUB radiograph

<!-- image -->

## Acute Cholecystitis: Diagnosis

## Chronic Cholecystitis

- AKA: gallbladder dyskinesia or biliary colic
- Smoldering course alternating with acute biliary colic $ May lead to acute cholecystitis
- Risk factors: female, obese, pregnancy, advancing age
- Imaging
- $ Abdominal US
- $ Cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan)

## QUESTION #4

A 13-year-old male presents to the clinic accompanied by his parent with reports of abdominal pain, nausea, and fever. On exam, Markle's sign is positive. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?

1. Urinary tract infection
2. Viral gastroenteritis
3. Acute appendicitis
4. Small bowel obstruction

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Acute Appendicitis

## QUESTION #5

A 42-year-old patient with a past medical history of smoking presents to the clinic with symptoms of pyrosis and regurgitation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1. Pyloric stenosis
2. Small bowel obstruction
3. Gastroesophageal reflux disease
4. Cholelithiasis

## Pathophysiology of GERD

- Retrograde flow of gastric contents into esophagus
- $ Poor esophageal motility
- $ Dysfunctional lower esophageal sphincter (LES)
- $ Increased volume and pressure in the stomach

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

Reflux can be physiologic or pathologic.

## GERD: Diagnosis

## Presumptive diagnosis

- Pathologic symptoms
- Symptoms occur ≥2 days per week
- Absence of alarm features

## Treatment:

- Weight loss (if appropriate)
- Dietary Modifications
- First-Line: PPIs

## GERD: Alarm Symptoms

- New onset age-60 years or older
- Evidence of GI bleeding (or new IDA)
- Anorexia/weight loss
- Dysphagia/odynophagia
- Vomiting (obstruction)
- GI cancer in first-degree relative 

## REFER!

## QUESTION #6

A 41-year-old female has had heartburn and regurgitation at night for the past month. She has no alarm symptoms. Which of the following actions should be taken?

1. Start the patient on an H2 blocker for 8 weeks.
2. Start the patient on a PPI for 8 weeks.
3. Refer the patient for an endoscopy to confirm the diagnosis of GERD.
4. Ensure that a pregnancy test is completed before initiating GERD treatment.

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES GERD TREATMENT

First-line pharmacologic management of GERD is PPIs.

| Class                        | Examples                                                                                                                    | Mechanism of Action                                                                        |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Antacids (PRN)               | · Maalox, Mylanta, Rolaids, Tums                                                                                            | · Increases pH for 20-30 minutes · Fastest relief                                          |
| H2 receptor antagonists      | · Cimetidine (Tagamet) · Famotidine (Pepcid) · Nizatidine                                                                   | · Decreases acid production for 6-12 hours · Provides relief in 60 minutes                 |
| Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) | · Omeprazole (Prilosec) · Lansoprazole (Prevacid) · Rabeprazole (Aciphex) · Esomeprazole (Nexium) · Pantoprazole (Protonix) | · Reduces gastric acid secretion · Provides relief in 1 to 3 days · Prescribe 8-week trial |

TIP: If there is no symptom relief of GERD after 8 weeks on a PPI-REFER!

## QUESTION #7

The 41-year-old female responds well to esomeprazole. Her GERD symptoms have resolved during 8 weeks of therapy. What should be done next?

1. Continue the medication indefinitely.
2. Remove the diagnosis of GERD from the patient's chart.
3. Refer the patient for an endoscopy to confirm GERD.
4. Discontinue the medication and see if symptoms persist after 2 to 4 weeks.

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #8

A 62-year-old non-Hispanic white male with a history of smoking presents to the clinic. He has been taking an OTC PPI for heartburn for 5 years and reports worsening pyrosis and regurgitation. Which of the following is the biggest concern?

1. The patient could have bone loss from prolonged PPI use.
2. The patient could have Barrett's esophagus or esophageal cancer.
3. The patient may be taking his PPI incorrectly.
4. The patient could be experiencing angina.

## Barrett's Esophagus

<!-- image -->

Dysplasia of the esophagus that develops secondary to chronic GERD

## Barrett's Esophagus: Risk Factors

- Male sex
- Age 50 or older
- non-Hispanic White American
- Chronic GERD (5 to 10 years or more)
- Cigarette smoking
- Hiatal hernia
- History of Barrett's/esophageal cancer in a first-degree relative

## QUESTION #9

A 58-year-old male who eats a low-fiber diet presents to the clinic with moderate left lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and a temperature of 100.6°F. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1. Uncomplicated diverticulitis
2. Large bowel obstruction
3. Testicular torsion
4. Colorectal cancer

What test should be ordered to confirm?

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Diverticular Disease

## Diverticulitis Management

## ACP Guidelines (2021)

Managed outpatient:

- Antibiotics: selectively, not routinely
- Pain control
- Liquid diet: advance as tolerated in 2-3 days
- No repeat imaging required if improving
- Follow-up colonoscopy in 6-8 weeks if no colonoscopy in the past year

## IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (IBS)

<!-- image -->

- Crampy pain
- $ Location and character varies
- Stool: varies (normal, diarrhea, constipation)
- $ Mucus present in stools

## IBS Management

<!-- image -->

TIP: Abdominal pain and cramping-give anti-spasmodic

## Diarrhea

- Wide differential diagnosis
- $ Infectious
- $ Colitis
- $ Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
- $ Inflammatory bowel diseases
- Ulcerative colitis
- Crohn disease
- $ Many, many more

TIP: Get a good history.

## Diarrhea: History

- Duration of symptoms
- Frequency
- Associated symptoms
- Characteristics
- $ Small bowel: watery, large volume, cramping, bloating/gas
- $ Large bowel: frequent, regular, small volume; fever, mucus, blood

What are we most worried about with diarrhea?

- Other symptoms
- $ GERD symptoms
- $ Early satiety
- $ Nausea
- $ Chest pain
- Etiology: serotonin mediated (90% found in the gut!)

NOTES

## NOTES

## Infectious Diarrhea

- Viral: Norovirus, Rotavirus (most common)
- $ Self-limited
- Bacterial: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Clostridioides difficile, Staphylococcus, others
- $ Suspect if immunocompromised or severe illness lasting more than 1 week
- Parasitic: Giardia, others
- $ Suspect if immunocompromised, international travel, or poor sanitation

## Diarrhea Red Flags

- Rectal bleeding
- Nocturnal bowel movements
- Nocturnal or progressive abdominal pain
- Weight loss
- Anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, electrolyte disturbances

| Symptoms                                            | Differential Diagnosis                        |
|-----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Anal pain during defecation                         | Anal fissure, rectal carcinoma                |
| Night sweats, fever, weight loss                    | Malignancy, chronic infection or inflammation |
| Diarrhea preceding or accompanying passage of blood | Colitis                                       |
| Change in frequency or caliber of stools            | Malignancy                                    |

## Inflammatory Bowel Disease

## Two types:

- Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease
- Peak incidence: 15-30 years

## Presentation:

- Diarrhea, bloody stools, abdominal pain, tenesmus
- Fatigue, anemia, and sometimes weight loss

TIP: Recognize and refer to gastroenterology.

## QUESTION #10

Which of the following patients is most likely to have colorectal cancer?

1. A 30-year-old who has diarrhea five times daily for the past 4 months
2. A 48-year-old who has intermittent loose stools and constipation
3. A 50-year-old who is vegetarian and has tenesmus pain and fever for 3 days
4. A 55-year-old who smokes, recent constipation, and normochromic anemia

<!-- image -->

## Colorectal Cancer

- Second most common cause of cancer death in males; third in females
- 86% diagnosed before age 50 are symptomatic, have advanced disease, and a poor prognosis
- Screening:
- $ Average risk patients
- $ Start at age 45

<!-- image -->

## Colorectal Cancer (CRC)

- Most CRCs arise from adenomatous polyps (two-thirds of polyps)
- Polyp → dysplasia → cancer
- Usually takes at least 10 years

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## Colorectal Cancer (CRC) Screening

"The best test is the one the patient will complete!"

| Method                                         | Frequency             | Comments                                                                                                      |
|------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Guaiac fecal occult blood test (gFOBT) (stool) | Annually, 3 specimens | Guaiac-based fecal occult blood tests                                                                         |
| Fecal immunochemical test (FIT) (stool)        | Annually, 1 specimen  | Fecal immunochemical tests; more sensitive than FOBT                                                          |
| FIT DNA (stool) (Cologuard)                    | 1-3 years             | Improved sensitivity, lower specificity; more specific for colon-related occult blood (Average risk patients) |
| Colonoscopy                                    | Every 10 years        | Gold standard                                                                                                 |
| Flex sigmoidoscopy                             | Every 5 years         | Only IDs lesions up to splenic flexure                                                                        |

## NOTES

## NOTES Liver Function Tests

- Metabolism/Conversion
- $ Alanine transaminase/ aspartate transaminase (ALT/ AST)
- Synthetic activity
- $ Bile
- $ Albumin
- $ PT
- Excretory function
- $ Bilirubin
- $ Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)

## Functions of the healthy liver

<!-- image -->

## Liver Function Test Interpretation

| Elevations   | Consider                                                                     |
|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ALT and AST  | Liver injury, hepatitis, MAFLD, acute liver failure (more than 10 times ULN) |
| ALP          | Think bone disease, liver disease, obstructed bile ducts                     |
| Bilirubin    | RBC destruction, liver disease, bile duct obstruction, Gilbert disease       |
| PT/INR       | Cirrhosis, cancer originating in liver (in the setting of abnormal LFTs)     |
| Albumin      | Usually normal in liver disease                                              |

## Metabolic-Associated Fatty Liver Disease (MAFLD)

- Formerly called "Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease" (NAFLD)
- Incidence: 1/3 of total U.S. population, 2/3 of patients with diabetes
- Associated conditions: ASCVD, kidney disease, diabetes
- Untreated:

<!-- image -->

## Identifying & Managing MAFLD

## Step 1: ID At-Risk Patients

- Metabolic syndrome risk factors (at least 2)
- Type 2 DM
- Steatosis on imaging
- Elevated ALT/AST

## MAFLD Management

FIB-4 (<1.3) Low Risk

Primary care

## Management:

- Lifestyle interventions: physical activity, diet, alcohol avoidance
- Weight loss as needed (more than 7-10%)
- CVD risk reduction measures
- Diabetes management per ADA

## Viral Hepatitis

- ALT greater than AST
- Viral infection affecting the liver
- $ Five viral causative agents:
- $ A, B, C, D, E
- Hepatitis B, C, and D can cause chronic infections.

## Hepatitis Screening Guidelines

| Hepatitis Type   | Screening Guidelines                                                                                                                                                        |
|------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hepatitis A      | · No specific recommendations · Clinical decision-making based on risk: occupational, international travel, homelessness, males who have sex with males, injection drug use |
| Hepatitis B      | · One-time universal screening ≥18 years of age · UNLESS serologic evidence of immunity · Each pregnancy                                                                    |
| Hepatitis C      | · One-time universal screening ≥18 years of age · Each pregnancy · Annually for high-risk populations (e.g., IV drug use)                                                   |

## Step 2: History/Labs

- Heavy alcohol use?
- CBC
- LFTs
- Hepatitis panel

## Step 3: Noninvasive Testing

- Fib-4 score Calculated
- $ Age
- $ AST/ALT
- $ Platelets

## FIB-4 (>1.3) Refer to hepatology

- Most likely will require liver biopsy and/or pharmacologic management of fatty liver disease

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Hepatitis Markers: IgM, IgG

- Immunoglobulins = antibodies
- $ IgM (M = minute)
- First antibody to be produced during acute infection
- $ IgG (G = gone)
- Produced when the body has immunity, usually after the infection is gone

## Hepatitis A (HAV) Markers

| Marker                                | Interpretation                 |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| (+) anti-HAV IgG                      | Immune                         |
| (+) anti-HAV IgM                      | Acute infection                |
| (-) anti-HAV IgM and (-) anti-HAV IgG | No immunity, need immunization |

## QUESTION #11

A patient who has jaundice, fever, and vomiting has the following results. What is your interpretation?

- (+) IgM anti-HAV
- (-) IgG anti-HAV

## Hepatitis B Markers

| Marker       | What Is It?                              | What Does It Mean?                        |
|--------------|------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| HBsAg        | Hepatitis B surface antigen              | Infected (currently or in the past)       |
| Anti-HBs     | Hepatitis B surface antibody             | Immune (vaccine or recovery from disease) |
| Anti-HBc     | Total hepatitis B core antibody          | Current or previous infection             |
| IgM anti-HBc | IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen | Acute hepatitis B (≤6 months)             |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Hepatitis B

What does it mean if…

| (+) HBsAg        | Infected                        |
|------------------|---------------------------------|
| (-) anti-HBs     | No immunity                     |
| (+) anti-HBc     | Current or previous infection   |
| (+) IgM anti-HBc | Infected for less than 6 months |

## QUESTION #12

What does it mean if hepatitis B labs reveal…

- (-) HBsAg
- (-) anti-HBs
- (-) anti-HBc

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #13

What does it mean if hepatitis B labs reveal…

- (-) HBsAg
- (+) anti-HBs
- (-) anti-HBc

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #14

What does it mean if hepatitis B labs reveal…

- (+) HBsAg
- (-) anti-HBs
- (+) anti-HBc
- (-) IgM anti-HBc

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #15

What does it mean if hepatitis B labs reveal…

- (-) HBsAg
- (+) anti-HBs
- (+) anti-HBc

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES Summary of Hepatitis B Markers

| HBsAg   | Anti-HBc   | Anti-HBs   | IgM Anti-HBc   | Interpretation                                                                                                                                                                             |
|---------|------------|------------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -       | -          | -          | NA             | Susceptible, needs vaccine                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -       | +          | +          | NA             | Immune due to resolved infection                                                                                                                                                           |
| -       | -          | +          | NA             | Immune due to vaccination                                                                                                                                                                  |
| +       | +          | -          | +              | Acutely infected                                                                                                                                                                           |
| +       | +          | -          | -              | Chronically infected                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -       | +          | -          | -              | Interpretation unclear. Four possibilities: 1. Resolved infection (most common) 2. False-positive anti-HBc, thus susceptible 3. "Low level" chronic infection 4. Resolving acute infection |

## Hepatitis B Quick List

<!-- image -->

## GI Imaging Studies

| Imaging Study                | Use                                                               | Comments                                            |
|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Plain flat/upright abdominal | Ileus, bowel obstruction, perforation                             | Quick, cheap, readily available                     |
| Abdominal ultrasound         | Gallbladder, pelvic organs, appendix (pediatrics), kidneys, liver | Difficult with large BMI, noninvasive, no radiation |
| CT                           | Acute abdominal pain, diverticulitis                              | Oral contrast: GI tract IV contrast: GI vasculature |
| MRI                          | Hepatocellular carcinoma, metastatic disease                      | Not for acute setting                               |
| HIDA                         | Rule out cholecystitis                                            | Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA)             |
| EGD                          | Evaluate upper GI tract                                           | Invasive, anesthesia                                |
| Colonoscopy                  | Evaluate lower GI tract                                           | Invasive, bowel prep, anesthesia                    |

## EXAM CHECKLIST

- Abdominal pain: know differentials
- GERD
- Diarrhea
- Encopresis
- GI red flags
- Hepatitis
- IBS vs. IBD
- Diverticulitis
- Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
- Labs, imaging studies
- Know clinical presentation (subjective, objective findings)
- Know how to diagnose
- What's in differential diagnosis?
- Pharmacologic, nonpharmacologic management
- Follow-up care

<!-- image -->
